questions.title: Why isn't testimony that the defendant previously had the same gun barred by Rule 404(b) as propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the court's treatment of D.F.'s and C.F.'s testimony that they had seen Cutbank with the sawed-off rifle before the charged incident. My instinct was that evidence of prior acts is usually restricted by Rule 404(b), especially if it risks inviting the jury to think "he had a gun before, so he must have had it this time too." But the Eighth Circuit calls this "intrinsic evidence" and says it shows continuous possession and control of the same weapon. What exactly makes prior possession of the same firearm "intrinsic" rather than Rule 404(b) evidence? Is this basically an exception whenever the government can tie the prior act to the identical gun, or is there a narrower doctrinal rule here?

questions.title: How did the Confrontation Clause issue disappear just because the declarant later testified at trial?
questions.question_body: Before trial, the defense wanted an instruction telling the jury not to treat D.F.'s out-of-court statements to police as substantive evidence until D.F. herself testified. The court denied that request, and the opinion says there was no Confrontation Clause problem because D.F. later testified in person. I'm struggling with the timing issue. If officers repeat an accuser's statements before the accuser testifies, doesn't the jury still hear testimonial hearsay at that point? Does the later appearance of the declarant automatically cure any Sixth Amendment issue, or only if the defendant has a full opportunity to cross-examine her? Also, how do courts distinguish between testimony offered merely to explain police conduct and testimony that effectively conveys the truth of the accusation?

questions.title: Why wasn't the witness's statement that her sister was killed by a gun excluded under Rule 403?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination about inconsistent statements, D.F. explained that she was not familiar with guns and did not like guns because her sister had been killed by one. That seems very emotionally charged, and I would have thought the defense would have a strong Rule 403 argument that it was unfairly prejudicial in a felon-in-possession case involving an alleged domestic assault. The court says the testimony was responsive to cross-examination and that no unfair prejudice was apparent. Is the idea that the defense "opened the door" by pressing her about why her prior descriptions were inconsistent? More generally, how do appellate courts evaluate prejudice when testimony is sympathetic but not directly probative of an element of the offense?

questions.title: Why couldn't defense counsel impeach the witness by reading from the police report if the report described her prior inconsistent statements?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the district court let defense counsel ask C.F. about what she told police, but would not allow counsel to read portions of the police report into the record without proper foundation because the report was not authored by C.F. I'm confused about the mechanics here. If the goal is impeachment by prior inconsistent statement, why isn't it enough that the report memorializes what she allegedly said? Does the defense need to establish that C.F. adopted the report, or call the officer who wrote it, or satisfy some separate authentication requirement before using it as extrinsic impeachment evidence? I'm trying to understand the interaction between Rule 613 and authentication rules in this setting.

questions.title: How can the sentencing court use 'another felony offense' for § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) when the defendant wasn't separately convicted of that felony?
questions.question_body: At sentencing, the court applied the four-level enhancement for possessing the firearm "in connection with another felony offense," apparently based on the underlying conduct involving domestic abuse/kidnapping/assault, even though the opinion doesn't mention a separate conviction for those offenses in this federal case. The commentary says the enhancement applies regardless of whether a charge was brought or a conviction obtained. Is that common across the Guidelines? What standard of proof applies when the sentencing judge finds that separate felony conduct occurred, and what evidence can the court rely on? The opinion also notes that the PSR's factual statements were adopted without objection—does failing to object effectively concede those facts for Guidelines purposes?

questions.title: Why did the court treat Cutbank's § 3553(a) argument as a substantive-reasonableness issue instead of a Guidelines-calculation error?
questions.question_body: Cutbank argued that applying § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) produced a sentence greater than necessary under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a), especially because the ACCA guideline would have yielded a lower total offense level than the otherwise-applicable calculations. The Eighth Circuit responded that the district court first had to correctly calculate the Guidelines, then consider whether the § 3553(a) factors justified a variance, and it presumed the within-Guidelines sentence was reasonable. I'm having trouble seeing the boundary here. If the defendant's real complaint is that the enhancement overstates the seriousness of the conduct in light of the ACCA framework, is that purely a substantive reasonableness argument? Or could there be a doctrinal argument that the enhancement should not apply at all because it double counts conduct already captured elsewhere in the sentence?

questions.title: What does the harmless-error analysis mean when the court says the evidentiary rulings 'did not influence or had only a slight influence on the verdict'?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly brushes aside the evidentiary issues and ends by saying any error would have been harmless because the government's evidence was substantial. I understand harmless error in the abstract, but I'm confused about how searching the review actually is in a criminal case. Does the appellate court ask whether the verdict surely would have been the same, whether there was overwhelming evidence, or whether the challenged evidence likely affected the jury? And when the defendant argues cumulative error, how do courts decide whether a series of individually minor rulings adds up to substantial prejudice?
